entry.title: Music with Nex, Part 2 — Duration and Meter
entry.content:
Part 1 of this series gave us Pitch: how high a note sounds. This part covers how long it lasts. By the end we will have three classes: Duration, Meter and Bar. We will also hear a bar of triplets played correctly.

Look again at the play function from Part 1:

  let ticks_per_beat := 4
  let ticks := beats_each * ticks_per_beat

Length there is a count of MIDI ticks, and that count already means two things at once. MIDI’s “beat” is always a quarter note, whatever the time signature says. In 6/8 the beat a musician counts is a dotted quarter, but MIDI still counts quarters. On top of that, a tick count depends on a resolution that the composer doesn’t care about: a quarter note is 4 ticks at one resolution and 480 at another.

Musicians don’t think in ticks. They think in fractions of a whole note: a quarter, an eighth, a dotted half, a triplet eighth. So that is how we will store duration. Ticks come back only at the edge, when we hand the music to the audio library.

A helper with a contract of its own

Fractions need a greatest common divisor, so we start with a free function:

function gcd(a, b: Integer): Integer
require
  positive: a > 0 and b > 0
do
  let x := a
  let y := b
  from until y = 0 do
    let r := x % y
    x := y
    y := r
  end
  result := x
ensure
  positive_result: result > 0
  divides_both: a % result = 0 and b % result = 0
end

The precondition is narrower than it needs to be: gcd is perfectly well defined for zero and negative numbers. We narrow it on purpose. Durations are always positive, so no caller in this program needs anything else. If a later part needs gcd(0, n), we will widen it then, and every caller written so far stays correct, because a wider precondition accepts everything the narrower one did.

The postcondition is good enough but incomplete. It says the result is a common divisor, not the greatest one. Hold on to that, we will revisit it later in an exercise.

Duration: an exact fraction of a whole note

class Duration
  note "A length of time as an exact fraction of a whole note."
inherit Comparable

feature
  WHOLE = create Duration.fraction(1, 1)
  HALF = create Duration.fraction(1, 2)
  QUARTER = create Duration.fraction(1, 4)
  EIGHTH = create Duration.fraction(1, 8)
  SIXTEENTH = create Duration.fraction(1, 16)

  once numerator: Integer
  once denominator: Integer

create
  fraction(n, d: Integer)
  require
    positive_numerator: n > 0
    positive_denominator: d > 0
  do
    let g := gcd(n, d)
    numerator := n / g
    denominator := d / g
  ensure
    same_value: numerator * d = n * denominator
  end

feature
  plus(other: Duration): Duration
  alias "+"
  do
    result := create Duration.fraction(numerator * other.denominator + other.numerator * denominator,
      denominator * other.denominator)
  ensure
    longer_than_both: this < result and other < result
  end

  minus(other: Duration): Duration
  alias "-"
  require
    leaves_something: other < this
  do
    result := create Duration.fraction(numerator * other.denominator - other.numerator * denominator,
      denominator * other.denominator)
  ensure
    adds_back: result + other = this
  end

  times(k: Integer): Duration
  alias "*"
  require
    positive_factor: k > 0
  do
    result := create Duration.fraction(numerator * k, denominator)
  ensure
    not_shorter: this <= result
  end

  halved: Duration
  do
    result := create Duration.fraction(numerator, denominator * 2)
  ensure
    doubles_back: result * 2 = this
  end

  -- Half as long again: a dotted quarter is 3/8.
  dotted: Duration
  do
    result := create Duration.fraction(numerator * 3, denominator * 2)
  ensure
    half_again: result = this + halved
  end

  -- COUNT notes in the space of SPACE: a triplet is tuplet(3, 2).
  tuplet(count, space: Integer): Duration
  require
    at_least_two: count >= 2
    some_space: space >= 1
  do
    result := create Duration.fraction(numerator * space, denominator * count)
  ensure
    fills_the_space: result * count = this * space
  end

  compare(other: Any): Integer
  do
    if convert other to d: Duration then
      let mine := numerator * d.denominator
      let theirs := d.numerator * denominator
      if mine < theirs then
        result := -1
      elseif mine > theirs then
        result := 1
      else
        result := 0
      end
    end
  end

  to_string: String do
    result := "" + numerator + "/" + denominator
  end

invariant
  positive: numerator > 0 and denominator > 0
  lowest_terms: gcd(numerator, denominator) = 1
end

Four things in this class are worth a closer look.

The lowest_terms invariant is what makes = correct. Part 1 relied on Nex’s default equality, which compares objects field by field. For fractions that is only safe if every value has exactly one representation. Without the invariant, 2/8 and 1/4 would be different objects with different fields, and = would call them unequal. The constructor reduces every fraction, and the invariant promises that no Duration anywhere has escaped the reduction. So the default equals is right, and we never had to write our own.

> print(create Duration.fraction(2, 8))
1/4
> create Duration.fraction(2, 8) = Duration.QUARTER
true

There is no zero duration, and minus has to respect that. A note that lasts no time is not a note. The positive invariant rules it out, and that turns subtraction into a partial operation. QUARTER - HALF has no answer among durations, so minus says so up front:

> print(Duration.QUARTER - Duration.HALF)
Error: Precondition violation: leaves_something

Notice what the precondition does not say. It does not say “the result must be positive”. It speaks in terms the caller can check before calling: the thing you take away must be shorter than what you start with.

Postconditions describe; they don’t restate. plus could have promised the exact sum, but that would just copy the body into the ensure. longer_than_both is a weaker promise that would still catch the bugs we are likely to make: a sign error, a swapped numerator, or multiplying where we meant to add. minus goes further and ties itself to plus: whatever it returns, adding other back must give the original. We used the same trick with interval_to and transposed in Part 1.

tuplet is defined by what musicians mean by it. “Three in the space of two” is the postcondition, almost word for word: three of the result take as long as two of the original.

> let trip := Duration.EIGHTH.tuplet(3, 2)
> print(trip)
1/12
> trip * 3 = Duration.EIGHTH * 2
true
> Duration.QUARTER + Duration.EIGHTH = Duration.QUARTER.dotted
true

Meter: a time signature, not a fraction

A time signature looks like a fraction, and it is tempting to store it as a Duration. It isn’t one.

class Meter
  note "A time signature: how many beats fill a bar, and which note value is one beat."

feature
  FOUR_FOUR = create Meter.make(4, 4)
  THREE_FOUR = create Meter.make(3, 4)
  SIX_EIGHT = create Meter.make(6, 8)

  once beats: Integer
  once beat_unit: Integer

create
  make(b, unit: Integer)
  require
    some_beats: b >= 1 and b <= 32
    power_of_two_unit: unit = 1 or unit = 2 or unit = 4 or unit = 8 or unit = 16 or unit = 32
  do
    beats := b
    beat_unit := unit
  end

feature
  beat: Duration
  do
    result := create Duration.fraction(1, beat_unit)
  end

  bar_length: Duration
  do
    result := create Duration.fraction(beats, beat_unit)
  ensure
    beats_fill_the_bar: result = beat * beats
  end

  to_string: String do
    result := "" + beats + "/" + beat_unit
  end

invariant
  some_beats: beats >= 1 and beats <= 32
  power_of_two_unit: beat_unit = 1 or beat_unit = 2 or beat_unit = 4 or beat_unit = 8 or beat_unit = 16 or beat_unit = 32
end

Here is the difference:

> Meter.SIX_EIGHT.bar_length = Meter.THREE_FOUR.bar_length
true
> Meter.SIX_EIGHT = Meter.THREE_FOUR
false

A bar of 6/8 lasts exactly as long as a bar of 3/4, but they are different meters. 6/8 is two groups of three eighths; 3/4 is three quarters. They sound different, and composers choose between them deliberately. So Meter keeps beats and beat_unit exactly as given, with no reduction, and the default equality tells them apart.

That makes two classes that look alike and make opposite choices. Duration normalises because 2/8 and 1/4 are the same length of time. Meter must not normalise, because 6/8 and 3/4 are not the same meter. Which values to normalise is a design decision, not a detail of the code, and each class’s invariant writes that decision down where readers can find it.

Bar: always exactly full

A bar is a run of note values that fills one meter. This version is pure rhythm: no pitches and no rests yet. Part 4 puts pitches on it.

First, a small free function to add up a list of durations. Since there is no zero duration, an empty list has no total, which is enforced by the precondition:

function total_length(durations: Array[Duration]): Duration
require
  not_empty: durations.length > 0
do
  result := durations.get(0)
  from let k := 1 until k = durations.length do
    result := result + durations.get(k)
    k := k + 1
  end
end

Now the class:

class Bar
  note "One bar of rhythm: note values that exactly fill a meter."

feature
  once meter: Meter

private feature
  once rhythm: Array[Duration]

create
  make(m: Meter, durations: Array[Duration])
  require
    not_empty: durations.length > 0
    fills_the_bar: total_length(durations) = m.bar_length
  do
    meter := m
    rhythm := durations.slice(0, durations.length)
  end

feature
  count: Integer
  do
    result := rhythm.length
  end

  item(i: Integer): Duration
  require
    valid_index: i >= 0 and i < count
  do
    result := rhythm.get(i)
  end

  total: Duration
  do
    result := total_length(rhythm)
  end

invariant
  not_empty: count > 0
  full: total = meter.bar_length
end

> let waltz := create Bar.make(Meter.THREE_FOUR, [Duration.HALF, Duration.QUARTER])
> let jig := create Bar.make(Meter.SIX_EIGHT, [Duration.QUARTER.dotted, Duration.EIGHTH, Duration.EIGHTH, Duration.EIGHTH])
> create Bar.make(Meter.THREE_FOUR, [Duration.HALF, Duration.HALF])
Error: Precondition violation: fills_the_bar

As in Part 1, the precondition and the invariant say the same thing. The precondition tells the caller what to provide, and the invariant promises that it stays true. But the invariant will break if not for two small details that are easy to skip past: rhythm is private, and the constructor stores a copy of the array it was given.

Here is what happens without them. Suppose make kept the caller’s array instead (rhythm := durations):

> let pattern := [Duration.QUARTER, Duration.QUARTER, Duration.HALF]
> let bar := create Bar.make(Meter.FOUR_FOUR, pattern)
> pattern.add(Duration.QUARTER)
> bar.count
Error: Class invariant violation: full

Nothing is wrong with count, and nothing was wrong when the bar was created. The bar was changed from outside, through an array it shared with its creator, and nobody told it. Nex checks invariants on the way out of every qualified call, so the damage is reported at the next call on the bar, which can be far from the line that did it. once doesn’t help here: it stops rhythm from being reassigned, but it doesn’t stop anyone from changing what is inside it.

The rule this teaches is one of the most important in object-oriented design: an invariant can only protect state that the class owns. If others can reach a class’s insides, they can break its promises. slice gives the bar its own array, so changing pattern afterwards no longer reaches it. private feature closes the other door: if rhythm were public, any client could write bar.rhythm.add(...) and break the bar directly. Clients read the rhythm one note at a time through item, which hands out Duration values. Those can’t be changed, so sharing them is safe.

Back to ticks, and the bug a test suite would miss

Eventually the audio library needs integers. Here is the obvious conversion, added to Duration:

  to_ticks(ticks_per_quarter: Integer): Integer
  do
    result := numerator * ticks_per_quarter * 4 / denominator
  end

A whole note is four quarters, so this scales the fraction up and divides. Let’s test it the way most people would, at 4 ticks per quarter:

Duration Fraction Ticks at 4 per quarter
Quarter 1/4 4
Eighth 1/8 2
Dotted quarter 3/8 6
Half 1/2 8
Sixteenth 1/16 1

Every value is right, and every 4/4 bar built from them adds up to 16 ticks. The suite passes.

Now a bar of triplet eighths. The triplet is 1/12 of a whole note, and 1 × 4 × 4 / 12 is 16/12, which integer division turns into 1. Twelve triplets come to 12 ticks, not 16. The Bar is still full: its invariant holds, because the model is right. It is the conversion that loses time, and it does so silently. Every bar of triplets ends four ticks early, pulling in the next bar. After four bars of triplets, the music is a whole bar ahead of where it should be. Nothing fails. You just hear rushed triplets and wonder about your ears.

A test suite misses this because tests check examples, and this bug only shows up for examples nobody thought of. It needs a denominator that doesn’t divide 4 × ticks_per_quarter. Anyone who thought to write that test would have found the bug while writing the code. A contract doesn’t need anyone to think of the case. It states the rule for every case at once:

  to_ticks(ticks_per_quarter: Integer): Integer
  require
    positive_resolution: ticks_per_quarter > 0
    exact_in_ticks: (numerator * ticks_per_quarter * 4) % denominator = 0
  do
    result := numerator * ticks_per_quarter * 4 / denominator
  ensure
    no_rounding: result * denominator = numerator * ticks_per_quarter * 4
  end

Why a precondition and not just the postcondition? Ask who is at fault. The routine can’t do better: there is no whole number of ticks that equals a triplet at 4 per quarter. The caller picked a resolution that is too coarse for the music, so the caller is the one who should hear about it, at the call. The postcondition stays as the client-facing promise: whatever you get back was not rounded.

What resolution is enough? It depends on the music, which is exactly why it should be checked rather than guessed. 12 per quarter covers triplets and straight sixteenths. 480, a common choice in sequencers, also covers quintuplets and thirty-seconds. But 480 still fails for septuplets, because 1920 is not divisible by 28. The contract tells you so the first time a septuplet turns up.

Making it sound

To hear a bar, we play each note value as a drum hit, accenting the first note of every bar. The playback loop is the one from Part 1:

intern audio/Midi_Song

function play_bars(bars: Array[Bar], ticks_per_quarter: Integer)
require
  something_to_play: bars.length > 0
  positive_resolution: ticks_per_quarter > 0
do
  let score := create Midi_Score.make(ticks_per_quarter)
  let tick := 0
  across bars as bar do
    from let k := 0 until k = bar.count do
      let ticks := bar.item(k).to_ticks(ticks_per_quarter)
      let velocity := when k = 0 then 120 else 80 end
      score.add_note(Midi.DRUM_CHANNEL, Midi.COWBELL, velocity, tick, ticks)
      tick := tick + ticks
      k := k + 1
    end
  end
  let song := create Midi_Song.from_score(score)
  song.play()
  from until song.is_stopped() do
    song.update()
    sleep(20)
  end
  song.close()
end

let straight := create Bar.make(Meter.FOUR_FOUR,
  [Duration.QUARTER, Duration.EIGHTH, Duration.EIGHTH, Duration.HALF])

let trip := Duration.EIGHTH.tuplet(3, 2)
let triplets: Array[Duration] := []
repeat 12 do
  triplets.add(trip)
end
let rolling := create Bar.make(Meter.FOUR_FOUR, triplets)

play_bars([straight, rolling, straight, rolling], 4)

Run it at 4 ticks per quarter and it stops before playing a note:

Error: Precondition violation: exact_in_ticks

Change the last line to play_bars([straight, rolling, straight, rolling], 12) and the triplets roll evenly, every bar the same length.

The failure is the program working as intended. The precondition turned a subtle timing bug into a one-line error message, before a single wrong note was played.

What the contracts bought us

  • An invariant can justify a shortcut. lowest_terms is the reason we could use Nex’s default equality for Duration without writing our own.
  • Invariants record design decisions. Duration normalises and Meter doesn’t, and each class says so in a place readers will look.
  • An invariant only protects what the class owns. Bar keeps its promise because its rhythm is private and copied in. Shared, mutable state is how invariants get broken from the outside.
  • Contracts cover the cases nobody thought to test. exact_in_ticks is a rule about every duration, not an example of one, and it names the caller who chose the wrong resolution.

Next: Scale and Chord

We have pitches, and we have time. Part 3 builds harmony on top of Pitch and Interval: a Scale as a set of steps from a tonic, and a Chord whose tones are checked against it.

Try it yourself

  1. gcd’s postcondition is satisfied by result := 1. Replace the body with exactly that and see what happens to Duration. Does any contract fail? Then write a postcondition that rules the fake body out. (Hint: what is true of a / result and b / result when result really is the greatest common divisor?)
  2. Write smallest_resolution(bars: Array[Bar]): Integer, the least number of ticks per quarter that renders every note in bars exactly. What should its postcondition promise, in terms of to_ticks?
  3. Add Meter.is_compound (true for 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8) and a beat_group: Duration that returns a dotted quarter for compound meters and the plain beat otherwise. Which contract connects beat_group to bar_length?

entry.title: Music with Nex, Part 1 — Pitch and Interval
entry.summary: The first part of a series that builds a small music sequencer from scratch in Nex.
entry.content:
The goal of this series is to build a small music sequencer from scratch in Nex. By the last part it will let you sketch phrases on a piano roll, generate melodies, and play them back. But the real aim is to show you the Nex way of writing object-oriented code where every class states what it promises, and Nex checks the promises while the program runs.

Music is a good test bed for this. It is full of rules that are easy to state and easy to break. For instance, a bar must add up to its time signature and a transposed melody must stay inside the instrument’s range. As we build the sequencer in small steps, we will see how contracts help up express these facts in a clear and enforceable way.

Nex already ships an audio library with a General MIDI synthesizer, a score you can fill note by note, and a player. So we will not write a single line of sound plumbing. Our job is the layer above it: the musical ideas captured as classes with contracts.

We start with two basic musical ideas: the pitch and interval. A pitch is how high a note sounds. An interval is the distance between two pitches. By the end of this part you will have two small classes, Pitch and Interval, and a C major scale playing through your speakers.

The trouble with raw integers

Here is how the audio library wants a note:

intern audio/Midi_Song

let score := create Midi_Score.make(4)      -- 4 ticks to a beat
score.add_note(0, 60, 90, 0, 4)            -- channel, pitch, velocity, start, length

That call is already guarded by contracts. add_note requires the channel to be in 0..15, the pitch and velocity in 0..127, the start not negative and the length positive. Break any of those and you get a precondition violation naming the rule.

But look at what the guard cannot see. Every argument is an Integer. Swap the pitch and the velocity and the call still passes every check:

score.add_note(0, 90, 60, 0, 4)            -- meant middle C at velocity 90

That plays the F# two and a half octaves above middle C, quietly. Nothing complains, because 90 is a perfectly good pitch and 60 an equally good velocity.

The second problem is distance. Suppose a melody is stored as integers and we transpose it up an octave by adding 12. A note at 120 becomes 132. Nothing notices until rendering, when add_note rejects it, far from the line that made the mistake. The error names add_note, not the transposition.

Both problems have the same cure: give the idea its own class. A Pitch cannot be passed where a velocity is expected, and a Pitch that would leave the MIDI range cannot be created. The check moves from the edge of the program to the moment the mistake is made.

Pitch: a value that cannot be wrong

A pitch is a value, like a number or a colour. Two middle Cs are the same pitch, and a pitch never changes once it exists. Here is the whole class. Read the contracts first; then the bodies.

intern Interval

class Pitch
  note "How high a note sounds: one of the 128 MIDI pitches, middle C = 60."
inherit Comparable

feature
  LOWEST = 0
  HIGHEST = 127
  LETTER_STEPS = {"C": 0, "D": 2, "E": 4, "F": 5, "G": 7, "A": 9, "B": 11}
  SHARP_NAMES = ["C", "C#", "D", "D#", "E", "F", "F#", "G", "G#", "A", "A#", "B"]

  once midi: Integer

create
  from_midi(n: Integer)
  require
    in_midi_range: n >= LOWEST and n <= HIGHEST
  do
    midi := n
  end

  -- Scientific pitch notation: middle C is ("C", 0, 4).
  -- accidental counts sharps (+) or flats (-).
  named(letter: String, accidental, oct: Integer)
  require
    one_letter: letter.length = 1 and "CDEFGAB".contains(letter)
    plain_accidental: accidental >= -2 and accidental <= 2
    octave_in_range: oct >= -1 and oct <= 9
    not_below_c_minus_1: oct > -1 or LETTER_STEPS.get(letter) + accidental >= 0
    not_above_g9: oct < 9 or LETTER_STEPS.get(letter) + accidental <= 7
  do
    this.from_midi((oct + 1) * 12 + LETTER_STEPS.get(letter) + accidental)
  end

feature
  -- Which of the twelve notes this is, C = 0 up to B = 11.
  pitch_class: Integer
  do
    result := midi % 12
  ensure
    one_of_twelve: result >= 0 and result <= 11
  end

  octave: Integer
  do
    result := midi / 12 - 1
  ensure
    rebuilds_midi: (result + 1) * 12 + pitch_class() = midi
  end

  name: String
  do
    result := SHARP_NAMES.get(pitch_class()) + octave()
  end

  -- Equal temperament, tuned to A4 = 440 Hz.
  frequency: Real
  do
    result := 440.0 * (2.0 ^ ((midi - 69).to_real / 12.0))
  ensure
    positive: result > 0.0
  end

  transposed(by: Interval): Pitch
  require
    stays_in_range: midi + by.semitones >= LOWEST
      and midi + by.semitones <= HIGHEST
  do
    result := create Pitch.from_midi(midi + by.semitones)
  ensure
    moved_by: result.midi - midi = by.semitones
  end

  interval_to(other: Pitch): Interval
  do
    result := create Interval.make(other.midi - midi)
  ensure
    lands_on_other: transposed(result) = other
  end

  compare(other: Any): Integer
  do
    if convert other to p: Pitch then
      if midi < p.midi then
        result := -1
      elseif midi > p.midi then
        result := 1
      else
        result := 0
      end
    end
  end

  to_string: String do
    result := name()
  end

invariant
  in_midi_range: midi >= LOWEST and midi <= HIGHEST
end

A few things are worth slowing down for.

The invariant and the precondition say the same thing, on purpose. The invariant is the class’s promise: no Pitch anywhere in the program is outside 0..127. The precondition on from_midi is the caller’s side of that bargain: don’t ask for one that is. If a caller breaks the rule, the error blames the caller, right at the call site:

> create Pitch.from_midi(128)
Error: Precondition violation: in_midi_range

named speaks the musician’s language and checks it in the musician’s terms. The range rule becomes three clauses about octaves: an octave must be -1..9, nothing goes below C-1, and nothing goes above G9. Each clause has a name, so a failure tells you which rule you broke, not just that some arithmetic went out of bounds. Note one_letter: "CDEFGAB".contains("") is true, so without the length check an empty string would slip through.

Postconditions document the arithmetic. octave uses integer division, and its postcondition says exactly what that division must get right: put the octave and the pitch class back together and you get the MIDI number again. A reader who doubts midi / 12 - 1 does not have to work it out. The class checks it every time.

Comparable buys ordering. Inheriting it and defining compare gives <, <=, > and >= on pitches. We will lean on that when we check that a melody stays inside an instrument’s range.

Try it:

> let c4 := create Pitch.named("C", 0, 4)
> c4.midi
60
> let a4 := create Pitch.named("A", 0, 4)
> a4.frequency
440.0
> c4 < a4
true
> c4 = create Pitch.from_midi(60)
true

Interval: distance and direction

An interval is a signed number of semitones. Up a fifth is +7; down a minor third is -3. Like Pitch, it is a value.

class Interval
  note "A signed distance between two pitches, in semitones."
inherit Comparable

feature
  once semitones: Integer

create
  make(n: Integer)
    require
      within_midi_span: n >= -127 and n <= 127
    do
      semitones := n
    end

feature
  UNISON = create Interval.make(0)
  MINOR_SECOND = create Interval.make(1)
  MAJOR_SECOND = create Interval.make(2)
  MINOR_THIRD = create Interval.make(3)
  MAJOR_THIRD = create Interval.make(4)
  PERFECT_FOURTH = create Interval.make(5)
  PERFECT_FIFTH = create Interval.make(7)
  OCTAVE = create Interval.make(12)

  is_ascending(): Boolean do result := semitones > 0 end
  is_descending(): Boolean do result := semitones < 0 end

  -- The same distance in the other direction.
  reversed(): Interval
  do
    result := create Interval.make(-semitones)
  ensure
    opposite: result.semitones = -semitones
  end

  plus(other: Interval): Interval
  alias "+"
  require
    stays_in_span: (semitones + other.semitones).abs <= 127
  do
    result := create Interval.make(semitones + other.semitones)
  ensure
    adds_up: result.semitones = semitones + other.semitones
  end

  -- Folded into one octave, as an upward step of 0..11 semitones.
  -- A tenth (16) folds to a major third (4).
  simple: Interval
  do
    result := create Interval.make(semitones % 12)
  ensure
    within_octave: result.semitones >= 0 and result.semitones <= 11
    same_class: (semitones - result.semitones) % 12 = 0
  end

  compare(other: Any): Integer
  do
    if convert other to i: Interval then
      if semitones < i.semitones then
        result := -1
      elseif semitones > i.semitones then
        result := 1
      else
        result := 0
      end
    end
  end

  to_string: String
  do
    result := "Interval(" + semitones + ")"
  end
end

plus is bound to + with alias, so Interval.OCTAVE + Interval.PERFECT_FIFTH reads like music theory and is still exactly a call to plus, precondition and all.

If you look carefully at simple you might see a problem: when we ask whether a note belongs to a chord, we care about the interval from the root folded into one octave. The body semitones % 12 looks right, and for upward intervals it is. Try a downward one:

> let tenth := create Interval.of(16)
> tenth.simple
Interval(4)
> let down := create Interval.of(-15)
> down.simple
Error: Postcondition violation: within_octave

Nex’s % keeps the sign of the dividend, as Java does, so -15 % 12 is -3, not 9. Without the postcondition, simple would quietly return Interval(-3), and the chord check two posts from now would decide that a perfectly good chord tone was wrong. With it, the routine that broke its promise is named at the moment it breaks it. The fix is one line:

      result := create Interval.make((semitones % 12 + 12) % 12)

The same_class clause is as important as within_octave. A body that returned Interval.UNISON every time would satisfy the range check. same_class rules that out: the folded interval must differ from the original by whole octaves.

Pitch meets Interval

Now let’s add two methods to Pitch to tie it together with Interval:

  transposed(by: Interval): Pitch
  require
    stays_in_range: midi + by.semitones >= LOWEST
      and midi + by.semitones <= HIGHEST
  do
    result := create Pitch.from_midi(midi + by.semitones)
  ensure
    moved_by: result.midi - midi = by.semitones
  end

  interval_to(other: Pitch): Interval
  do
    result := create Interval.make(other.midi - midi)
  ensure
    lands_on_other: transposed(result) = other
  end

The precondition on transposed is the cure for the second problem from the start of the post. Transposing a melody past the top of the range now fails on the line that transposes, not inside the renderer:

> let top_c := create Pitch.named("C", 0, 9)
> top_c.transposed(Interval.OCTAVE)
Error: Precondition violation: stays_in_range

The postcondition on interval_to is a different kind of promise. It does not restate the body; it ties two features together. Whatever interval_to returns, transposed must undo it. If either routine changes later, this one line keeps them in sync.

Why not a mutable transpose?

It is tempting to write a command instead, one that changes the pitch in place:

  transpose(by: Interval)
  require
    stays_in_range: midi + by.semitones >= LOWEST
      and midi + by.semitones <= HIGHEST
  do
    midi := midi + by.semitones
  ensure
    moved_by: midi = old midi + by.semitones
  end

The contract is fine; old midi is exactly the right tool for a command. Nex rejects the class anyway, because midi is a once field. This is a deliberate design choice. If pitches could change, then a Phrase holding the same Pitch object in two places would have both notes move when you transpose one. Values that cannot change can be shared freely, and that will make every collection class later in the series simpler. We will have appropriate use for old later when we implement Phrase and Voice which are things that do change.

Making it sound

A major scale is a pattern of steps: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. In our terms that is a list of intervals, and building the scale is a walk from the tonic:

let whole := Interval.MAJOR_SECOND
let half := Interval.MINOR_SECOND
let major_steps: Array[Interval] := [whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half]

let scale: Array[Pitch] := [create Pitch.named("C", 0, 4)]
across major_steps as step do
  scale.add(scale.get(scale.length - 1).transposed(step))
end

across scale as p do print(p.name) end
-- C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 B4 C5

To hear it, we hand the pitches to the audio library. This is the only place in this part where a Pitch turns back into an Integer, and it does so at the last possible moment, inside one small function:

intern audio/Midi_Song

function play(pitches: Array[Pitch], beats_each: Integer)
require
  something_to_play: pitches.length > 0
  positive_length: beats_each > 0
do
  let ticks_per_beat := 4
  let ticks := beats_each * ticks_per_beat
  let score := create Midi_Score.make(ticks_per_beat)
  score.set_instrument(0, Midi.PIANO, 0)
  from let k := 0 until k = pitches.length do
    score.add_note(0, pitches.get(k).midi, 90, k * ticks, ticks)
    k := k + 1
  end
  let song := create Midi_Song.from_score(score)
  song.play()
  from until song.is_stopped() do
    song.update()
    sleep(20)
  end
  song.close()
end

play(scale, 1)

Notice what can no longer go wrong at the add_note call. The pitch argument comes from a Pitch, so it is in range by the class invariant; add_note’s own valid_pitch check can never fire from here. The velocity and pitch can still be swapped by hand in this one function, but there is now exactly one place to look. In a later part of the series we will replace this function with a proper Renderer class and a contract that checks the score against the model.

No speakers, or running on a server? Set NEX_AUDIO=off. The library plays silently and the contracts are checked all the same.

What the contracts bought us

Two small classes, and already three kinds of protection:

  • Types keep ideas apart. A Pitch cannot be passed where a velocity or a channel is expected. No contract could catch the swapped arguments from the start of this post; a class does it for free.
  • Preconditions put the blame at the call. An out-of-range pitch or transposition fails on the line that asked for it, with a rule name that says what was wrong.
  • Postconditions catch the code we were sure of. simple was one line, it looked right, and it was wrong for every descending interval. The postcondition found it the first time a descending interval came through.

So the take away is: types say what a thing is; contracts say what must be true of it. Each catches what the other cannot.

Next: Duration and Meter

Pitch is half of a note. Part 2 adds the other half: how long it lasts. We will represent durations as exact fractions of a whole note rather than MIDI ticks, give Meter an invariant that every bar is full, and meet the first contract that a test suite would almost certainly miss.

Try it yourself

  1. Add Pitch.named_flat that spells pitches with flats (Db rather than C#). What should its postcondition promise about midi?
  2. Give Interval a name query that returns “M3”, “P5” and so on for simple intervals. Which precondition does it need, and could simple remove the need for one?
  3. Remove the same_class clause from simple and write a wrong body that still passes within_octave. How many tests would you need to catch it instead?

entry.title: Handling command-line arguments in Nex
entry.summary: A Nex program reads its arguments from the predeclared program object. Here is how to get at them, parse them into usable formats, and deal with invalid input gracefully.
entry.content:
Every Nex program starts with two objects already declared: console, for reading and writing text, and program, which describes the running program. program.arguments returns the command-line arguments as an Array[String].

let args: Array[String] := program.arguments

console.print_line("got " + args.length + " argument(s)")
across args as a do
  console.print_line("  " + a)
end

Updated 22 October 2026: this post now uses the predeclared program and console, which arrive in the release after 0.6.2. On 0.6.2 itself, declare them yourself: (create Process).command_line() returns the same arguments, and create Console makes a console.

Save that as args.nex and run it with a few arguments:

$ nex args.nex report.txt "two words" --top 3
got 4 argument(s)
  report.txt
  two words
  --top
  3

Three things to notice:

  • The array holds only your arguments. It starts after the file name, so there is no argv[0] to skip, and with no arguments it is empty.
  • The shell has already split the words. "two words" arrives as one element.
  • Everything is a String. 3 is text until you call to_integer on it.

Reserved runtime flags

nex takes a few options of its own, such as --interpret, --skip-contracts and --classpath. It removes them from the command line wherever they appear, so your program never sees them:

$ nex args.nex one --interpret two --skip-contracts three
got 3 argument(s)
  one
  two
  three

As those names are taken by the runtime, you cannot reuse them as your own options.

A small tool

Here is a complete program that greets someone, with an optional repeat count and an option to shout.

-- greet: say hello from the command line.
--
--   nex greet.nex <name> [--times n] [--shout]

class Options
feature
  name: String
  times: Integer
  shout: Boolean
create
  make(a_name: String, a_times: Integer, a_shout: Boolean)
  require
    has_name: a_name.length > 0
    positive_times: a_times > 0
  do
    name := a_name
    times := a_times
    shout := a_shout
  end
invariant
  has_name: name.length > 0
  positive_times: times > 0
end

function fail(message: String) do
  console.error("greet: " + message)
  console.error("usage: nex greet.nex <name> [--times n] [--shout]")
  exit(2)
end

function to_count(text: String): Integer
do
  result := text.to_integer()
  if result <= 0 then
    fail("--times must be at least 1, got " + text)
  end
rescue
  fail("--times needs a whole number, got " + text)
end

function parse(args: Array[String]): Options
do
  let name: String := ""
  let times: Integer := 1
  let shout: Boolean := false
  let i: Integer := 0
  from
    i := 0
  until
    i = args.length
  do
    let arg: String := args.get(i)
    if arg = "--shout" then
      shout := true
    elseif arg = "--times" then
      if i + 1 = args.length then
        fail("--times needs a value")
      end
      i := i + 1
      times := to_count(args.get(i))
    elseif arg.starts_with("--") then
      fail("unknown option " + arg)
    elseif name = "" then
      name := arg
    else
      fail("unexpected argument " + arg)
    end
    i := i + 1
  end
  if name = "" then
    fail("missing <name>")
  end
  result := create Options.make(name, times, shout)
end

function main() do
  let opts: Options := parse(program.arguments)
  let greeting: String := "Hello, " + opts.name + "!"
  if opts.shout then
    greeting := greeting.to_upper()
  end
  let n: Integer := 0
  from
    n := 0
  until
    n = opts.times
  do
    console.print_line(greeting)
    n := n + 1
  end
end

main()

It behaves the way you would expect a command-line tool to behave:

$ nex greet.nex Ada
Hello, Ada!

$ nex greet.nex Ada --times 3 --shout
HELLO, ADA!
HELLO, ADA!
HELLO, ADA!

$ nex greet.nex Ada --times zero
greet: --times needs a whole number, got zero
usage: nex greet.nex <name> [--times n] [--shout]

$ nex greet.nex Ada --loud
greet: unknown option --loud
usage: nex greet.nex <name> [--times n] [--shout]

The program is short, but there are some patterns worth copying.

Parse once, at the edge

main does not pass the raw array around. It calls parse once and from then on works with an Options object. No other part of the program looks at strings, checks whether an index is in range, or wonders whether times was converted yet.

Bad input is not a bug

Someone typing --times zero has made a mistake, but the program is fine. So parse handles it with ordinary code: it prints a message that names the problem, prints the usage line, and stops. to_integer() raises a Conversion_Error on text that is not a number, and the rescue clause in to_count turns that into the same kind of message.

Errors go to console.error, which writes to standard error, so they stay out of the way when the output is piped somewhere. exit(2) sets the exit status. By convention 0 means success and 2 means the command was used wrongly, which lets a shell script tell the two apart.

A broken parser is a bug

The contracts on Options do a different job. They are not there to check the user. They state what the rest of the program may assume: there is a name, and times is positive. main relies on that when it loops opts.times times without checking anything.

That makes the constructor a checkpoint for the parser itself. Suppose a later edit drops the result <= 0 test from to_count. Nothing about the type of times changes, and the program still compiles. But the first run with a bad value stops at the boundary:

$ nex greet.nex Ada --times 0
Error: Precondition violation: positive_times
  The call at line 70, in parse does not meet the precondition `positive_times` of Options.make.
  called from line 74, in main
  called from line 90

The message names the clause and blames the caller, parse, which is where the missing check belongs. A user should never see this message. If one does, it is telling you about a hole in your validation, not about their typing.

File arguments and relative paths

One thing will surprise you the first time you take a file name as an argument. The nex launcher starts your program from its own installation directory, so a relative path like report.txt does not resolve against the directory you ran the command in. The launcher records that directory, and program.working_directory gives it back to you, so you can resolve the path yourself:

function resolve(raw: String): String
do
  if raw.starts_with("/") then
    result := raw
  else
    result := program.working_directory + "/" + raw
  end
end

The same code is right for the next section too: a compiled program does not go through the launcher, and there working_directory is simply the directory the program runs in.

Shipping it as a jar

nex compile jvm turns the program into a standalone jar. The arguments reach it the same way, so nothing in the code changes:

$ nex compile jvm greet.nex
$ java -jar greet.jar Grace --times 2
Hello, Grace!
Hello, Grace!

Where to go next

  • program can also read the environment (env, has_env) and end the program with a status (exit), and Process starts child processes. The full list is in the system classes reference.
  • If require, ensure and invariant are new to you, the tour of Nex introduces them in a few minutes.
